questions.prompt: After lunch, Tom took his dog for the walk.

questions.prompt: If the weather was sunny, we would go hiking.

questions.prompt: The house looks new since it was painting last year.

questions.prompt: Almost every afternoon, Bill is stopping at the store.

questions.prompt: At this concert, the best performers is the last group.
questions.explanation: Plural subject requires 'are'.

questions.prompt: Their commute is long, but they says it is worth it.
questions.explanation: Plural subject takes 'say'.

items.transcript: Lecture. Professor: Today we will discuss riparian rights, which involve legal rights related to land next to rivers, lakes, and streams. These rights include access to water and limits on how landowners may use it. Modern law increasingly considers ecological impacts, because pollution in one area can affect entire water systems. Courts now balance private property interests with public health and environmental sustainability. This is why riparian law continues to evolve with scientific knowledge.

questions.prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: The legal meaning of riparian rights
questions.explanation: The professor explains riparian rights and their evolution.

questions.prompt: Why do modern courts consider ecology in these cases?
options: Because water impacts spread across systems
questions.explanation: Pollution can affect larger hydrologic systems.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about riparian law?
questions.explanation: He says it continues to evolve with science.

questions.prompt: What do riparian rights include?
options: Access to water and limits on its use
questions.explanation: The professor says these rights include access to water and limits on how landowners may use it.

questions.prompt: The word 'ecological' in the lecture is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Ecological relates to the environment and natural systems.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about how riparian law develops?
options: It was settled in the 19th century
It evolves with science and public health needs
It applies only to private farms
questions.explanation: The professor implies law evolves alongside scientific knowledge and public health concerns.

passages.title: Animal Behavior and Emotion
passages.text:
Scientists debate whether animal behavior is purely instinctive or sometimes reflects higher-order thinking. Many researchers agree that animals can feel pain, yet some remain uncertain about emotions such as grief or empathy because these are difficult to measure directly.

Other scientists argue that emotion can be inferred through behavior. For example, when one animal responds to another's distress in a way that reduces suffering, researchers may interpret that response as evidence of empathy. Critics of this interpretation say that such reactions may simply follow learned cues or biological triggers rather than conscious emotional choices. The debate continues because both sides rely on indirect evidence, and improved observation methods are still developing.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A debate about animal emotion and behavior
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts views on instinct vs emotion.

questions.prompt: Why do some scientists doubt animal emotions?
options: Emotions are hard to observe directly
questions.explanation: The text says emotions are difficult to measure.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about current evidence?
options: It is based only on lab experiments
questions.explanation: Both sides rely on indirect evidence.

questions.prompt: The word inferred in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Infer means conclude from evidence.

passages.title: Coffee and Society
passages.text:
Coffee is consumed daily by millions of people around the world and has become an important part of social and economic life. Historians disagree on the exact origin story, but most accounts place coffee's early use in East Africa before it spread through trade routes to the Middle East and Europe. [A] Over time, coffeehouses became places where people met to discuss politics, business, and culture.

Coffee production involves several stages. [B] After harvesting, beans are separated from the fruit, dried, roasted, and ground before brewing. Roasting is especially important because it changes flavor, aroma, and color. [C] Beyond taste, coffee also contains caffeine, which affects alertness and concentration. Today, coffee remains one of the most traded agricultural products globally, and modern cafes continue the historical role of serving as community gathering spaces. [D]

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Coffee is only a modern beverage
Coffee has historical, social, and economic importance
questions.explanation: The passage covers history, process, and social role.

questions.prompt: At what stage do beans change color significantly?
questions.explanation: Roasting changes flavor, aroma, and color.

questions.prompt: What role did historical coffeehouses often play?
options: Places for social and intellectual exchange
questions.explanation: The text says people met to discuss ideas and trade.

questions.prompt: What does the passage imply about coffee today?
options: It still has a social function
It is less traded than tea
questions.explanation: Modern cafes continue historical gathering functions.

questions.prompt: The word stages is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Stages means steps in a process.

questions.prompt: Where would this sentence most logically occur in relation to the marked sentences? "These spaces often hosted writers, merchants, and political thinkers discussing current events."
questions.explanation: The sentence expands the social role of coffeehouses and fits best after the idea introduced near [A].

tests.title: iTEP Practice Test III
instructions: This exam follows an iTEP-style format with five sections.
Complete sections in order and manage your time carefully.
Listening is forward-only and each audio can be played once.
Speaking allows one recording per task.

questions.prompt: My brother always ___ breakfast before going to work.
questions.explanation: Third-person singular present simple requires -s.

questions.prompt: She wants to become ___ architect when she graduates.
questions.explanation: Use 'an' before a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: By the time we arrived, the concert ___ already started.
questions.explanation: Past perfect (had + past participle) for an action completed before another past action.

questions.prompt: The meeting is scheduled ___ Monday morning.
questions.explanation: Use 'on' with specific days of the week.

questions.prompt: The annual report ___ by the finance department every December.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive for a regular, habitual action.

questions.prompt: The student ___ scored highest on the exam received a full scholarship.
questions.explanation: 'Who' refers to a person as the subject of the relative clause.

questions.prompt: She cannot come to the phone right now because she ___ a shower.
questions.explanation: Present continuous describes an action happening at the moment of speaking.

questions.prompt: The manager told his team that the project ___ completed by Friday.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' shifts to 'would'.

questions.prompt: The doctor recommended that he ___ more water every day.
questions.explanation: After 'recommend', use the base form (subjunctive mood).

questions.prompt: If she ___ more time, she would travel around the world.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: if + past simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: This is ___ interesting book I have ever read.
questions.explanation: Superlative adjectives require 'the most'.

questions.prompt: She ___ already submitted her application to three universities.
questions.explanation: Present perfect with 'already': third-person singular uses 'has'.

questions.prompt: Not until he read the full report ___ the severity of the problem.
questions.explanation: After negative adverbials like 'Not until', subject-auxiliary inversion is required.

questions.prompt: The news are very surprising to everyone in the community.
questions.explanation: 'News' is uncountable and takes a singular verb: 'is'.

questions.prompt: My friend and me planned a trip to the mountains last summer.
questions.explanation: Subject of the verb requires subject pronoun: 'I', not 'me'.

questions.prompt: This exercise is more easier than the one we did before.
questions.explanation: 'Easier' is already comparative; 'more' is redundant.

questions.prompt: She have been working at this company since 2018.
questions.explanation: Third-person singular requires 'has been', not 'have been'.

questions.prompt: If I would know the answer, I would tell you immediately.
questions.explanation: Second conditional if-clause requires past simple: 'knew', not 'would know'.

questions.prompt: The announcement will announced at tomorrow's press conference.
questions.explanation: Passive voice requires auxiliary 'be': 'will be announced'.

questions.prompt: He is best student in the entire class.
questions.explanation: Superlative adjectives require the definite article: 'the best student'.

questions.prompt: She arrived to the conference center before anyone else.
questions.explanation: Use 'at' with specific locations: 'arrived at', not 'arrived to'.

questions.prompt: You don't must eat or drink inside the library.
questions.explanation: Prohibition is expressed with 'must not' or 'mustn't', not 'don't must'.

questions.prompt: She spends her weekends reading, cooking, and to paint.
questions.explanation: Parallel structure requires the gerund: 'painting', not the infinitive 'to paint'.

questions.prompt: I do not understand what does he mean by that comment.
questions.explanation: Indirect questions use statement word order: 'what he means', not 'what does he mean'.

questions.prompt: Despite of the heavy traffic, she arrived at the meeting on time.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' does not take 'of'; use 'despite' alone or 'in spite of'.

items.transcript: Lecture. Professor: Good morning everyone. Today we will discuss the impact of urbanization on biodiversity. As cities expand, natural habitats are destroyed or fragmented, making it difficult for many species to survive. However, some research suggests that well-planned urban green spaces, such as parks and rooftop gardens, can support a surprising variety of wildlife. Certain bird species, insects, and small mammals have adapted to urban environments and, in some cases, even thrive there. Scientists argue that city planners should consider ecological connectivity when designing new developments. This means creating corridors of green space that allow animals to move between habitat areas. Without such planning, urban expansion continues to be one of the main drivers of species loss worldwide.

questions.prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How to build more parks in cities
The effects of urbanization on biodiversity
Why some animals migrate to warmer climates
questions.explanation: The lecture discusses how urban expansion affects biodiversity and possible solutions.

questions.prompt: What does research suggest about urban green spaces?
options: They are too expensive to maintain
They can support a variety of wildlife
They are harmful to native plant species
questions.explanation: The professor says research suggests well-planned green spaces can support wildlife.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply city planners should do?
options: Build taller buildings to conserve land
Include green corridors in urban designs
Focus solely on human population needs
questions.explanation: The professor says planners should consider ecological connectivity, meaning green corridors in development plans.

questions.prompt: What are ecological corridors?
options: Roads designed to reduce city traffic
Green pathways allowing animals to move between habitats
Areas reserved exclusively for urban farming
questions.explanation: The professor defines corridors as green spaces that allow animals to move between habitat areas.

questions.prompt: The word 'fragmented' in the lecture is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Fragmented' means divided or broken into disconnected pieces.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about urban expansion without ecological planning?
options: It benefits local wildlife over time
It is slowing down in most countries
It contributes to the loss of species
questions.explanation: The professor states that without proper planning, urban expansion is one of the main drivers of species loss.

passages.title: Urban Farming and Food Security
passages.text:
Urban farming — growing food in cities — has expanded rapidly in recent decades. Rooftop gardens, vertical farms, and community plots have emerged as responses to concerns about food security and the environmental impact of transporting food over long distances.

Supporters of urban farming argue that it reduces dependence on large agricultural operations and allows city residents to access fresher produce. Some research suggests that locally grown food retains more nutrients than food that has traveled hundreds of miles before reaching the consumer.

Critics, however, point out that urban farms currently produce only a small fraction of the food needed to sustain city populations. Land in cities is expensive, and the cost of setting up and maintaining urban farms can be high. Others argue that traditional agriculture remains more efficient for large-scale production.

Despite these challenges, many urban governments are investing in food-growing initiatives as part of broader sustainability efforts. Whether urban farming will become a significant part of the food supply remains to be seen.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A new type of city restaurant
Urban farming and its advantages and challenges
How to grow plants indoors without sunlight
Why cities are experiencing food shortages
questions.explanation: The passage presents urban farming from multiple perspectives, discussing both benefits and drawbacks.

questions.prompt: What do supporters of urban farming claim?
options: It is always cheaper than traditional farming
It reduces dependence on large farms and provides fresher food
It already produces most of a city's food supply
questions.explanation: Supporters say urban farming reduces dependence on large operations and offers fresher produce.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the critics' arguments?
options: Urban farming is not worth pursuing at all
Urban farming alone cannot currently feed a city
City land is becoming more affordable
questions.explanation: Critics note that urban farms produce only a small fraction of what cities need, implying they cannot feed whole populations alone.

questions.prompt: The word 'sustain' in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Sustain' means to maintain or support over time.

passages.title: The History of Vaccination
passages.text:
Vaccination is one of the most effective public health tools ever developed. The practice of introducing weakened or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate an immune response dates back centuries. Early forms of immunization were recorded in China and the Ottoman Empire before the concept reached Europe.

The English physician Edward Jenner is often credited with pioneering modern vaccination in the late eighteenth century. [A] Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox appeared to be protected against the more dangerous smallpox. By introducing material from a cowpox lesion into a healthy person, he demonstrated that protection could be achieved. [B]

The development of vaccines accelerated dramatically in the twentieth century, leading to the control or elimination of diseases such as polio, measles, and smallpox. [C] The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, representing the first infectious disease to be eliminated through a global vaccination campaign. [D]

Today, global vaccination programs continue to prevent millions of deaths each year, and ongoing research is expanding the range of diseases for which effective vaccines are available.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Vaccines are no longer necessary in the modern world
Vaccination has a long history and has saved millions of lives
Vaccines were first invented in the twentieth century
Smallpox remains a major global health threat today
questions.explanation: The passage traces vaccination from ancient practices to its modern global impact.

questions.prompt: What was Edward Jenner's key observation?
options: That smallpox was more common than cowpox
That milkmaids who had cowpox appeared immune to smallpox
That vaccination was already common in ancient China
That polio could be prevented through a specific diet
questions.explanation: Jenner observed that milkmaids who had contracted cowpox seemed protected against smallpox.

questions.prompt: When did the World Health Organization declare smallpox eradicated?
questions.explanation: The passage states the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

questions.prompt: What does the passage imply about modern vaccination research?
options: It has stopped because most diseases are under control
It is expanding to cover more diseases
It focuses primarily on smallpox prevention
It has failed to produce effective new vaccines
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that research is expanding the range of diseases for which vaccines are available.

questions.prompt: The word 'eradicated' in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Eradicated' means completely destroyed or eliminated.

questions.prompt: Where would this sentence most logically appear? 'This discovery laid the groundwork for the science of immunology.'
questions.explanation: After Jenner demonstrated that protection could be achieved [B], it is logical to note that this discovery founded the science of immunology.

tests.title: iTEP Practice Test IV
instructions: This exam follows an iTEP-style format with five sections.
Complete sections in order and manage your time carefully.
Listening is forward-only and each audio can be played once.
Speaking allows one recording per task.

questions.prompt: She always ____ her homework before dinner.
questions.explanation: Third-person singular present simple requires -s.

questions.prompt: I saw ____ amazing movie last night. You should watch it.
questions.explanation: Use 'an' before a vowel sound. 'Amazing' begins with a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: They ____ here since they moved from Spain five years ago.
questions.explanation: Present perfect with 'since' for an action that started in the past and continues to the present.

questions.prompt: The museum opens ____ nine in the morning.
questions.explanation: Use 'at' with specific times.

questions.prompt: By the time they arrive, the chef ____ cooking dinner.
questions.explanation: Future perfect expresses an action completed before a specific future moment.

questions.prompt: The company decided ____ a new branch in the south of the city.
questions.explanation: 'Decide' is followed by the infinitive.

questions.prompt: The book ____ I borrowed from the library is very interesting.
questions.explanation: 'That' (or 'which') is used for things in a defining relative clause.

questions.prompt: The teacher said that the exam ____ the following morning.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' shifts to 'would'.

questions.prompt: Had she known about the cancellation, she ____ a different flight.
questions.explanation: Third conditional inverted form: 'had + past participle' in the if-clause, 'would have + past participle' in the result.

questions.prompt: The announcement ____ to all staff members by noon tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Future passive: 'will be + past participle'.

questions.prompt: Your apartment is much ____ than mine.
questions.explanation: Comparative adjective for one-syllable words: add -er.

questions.prompt: She ____ be at home now because her car is in the driveway.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a logical deduction about the present.

questions.prompt: Rarely ____ such a talented musician in this region.
questions.explanation: After 'Rarely', subject-auxiliary inversion is required.

questions.prompt: Each of the students are required to submit a written report.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and requires a singular verb: 'is required'.

questions.prompt: The scholarship was awarded to both Sarah and I.
questions.explanation: Object pronoun is required after a preposition: 'to both Sarah and me'.

questions.prompt: She is used to work late every Friday at the office.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' requires a gerund: 'used to working', not the infinitive.

questions.prompt: He answered the questions very careful during the interview.
questions.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the verb: 'carefully', not 'careful'.

questions.prompt: If the train would have been on time, we would not have missed the meeting.
questions.explanation: Third conditional if-clause requires past perfect: 'had been', not 'would have been'.

questions.prompt: The letters was delivered to the wrong address by the postman.
questions.explanation: Plural subject 'letters' requires plural passive: 'were delivered'.

questions.prompt: I don't know nothing about the new schedule changes.
questions.explanation: Double negatives are non-standard; use 'anything': 'I don't know anything'.

questions.prompt: She is very interested on learning about ancient history.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'interested in', not 'interested on'.

questions.prompt: They explained us how to use the new software at the workshop.
questions.explanation: 'Explain' requires the preposition 'to' with an indirect object: 'explained to us'.

questions.prompt: They spent their honeymoon in a countryside of southern France.
questions.explanation: 'Countryside' is an uncountable noun used with the definite article: 'in the countryside'.

questions.prompt: The board demands that the director submits a full financial report.
questions.explanation: After 'demand that', the subjunctive requires the base form: 'submit', not 'submits'.

questions.prompt: The new regulations require companies to reduce emissions, improving efficiency, and report annually.
questions.explanation: Parallel infinitive structure requires: 'to reduce...improve...and report' — not the gerund 'improving'.

A language exchange program at the library

questions.explanation: Student B says they could recruit volunteers from the university's education department.

items.transcript: Lecture. Professor: Today we will examine microplastics, which are tiny plastic particles smaller than five millimeters. These particles originate from two main sources: large plastic items that break down over time due to sunlight and physical wear, and microbeads, which are very small particles deliberately added to cosmetics and personal care products. Microplastics have been detected in oceans, rivers, soil, and even in the air we breathe. Scientists are particularly concerned about their impact on marine ecosystems, because small fish and invertebrates often ingest these particles mistakenly, which can damage their digestive systems and reduce reproductive rates. Microplastics can also enter the human food chain through seafood consumption. While research is still ongoing, early findings suggest that chronic exposure may pose health risks. Some governments have already banned microbeads in personal care products, but the broader problem of plastic pollution continues to require international cooperation and policy changes.

questions.prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: Microplastics, their origins, and their effects
questions.explanation: The lecture covers what microplastics are, where they come from, and their environmental and health impacts.

options: Large plastic items breaking down and microbeads in personal care products

questions.explanation: The professor mentions degraded plastic items and microbeads deliberately added to cosmetics.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about the full health impact of microplastics on humans?
options: It is now fully established by research
It is not yet fully understood
It has been proven to cause serious illness
It only affects people who eat seafood daily
questions.explanation: The professor says research is still ongoing and findings 'suggest' risks, implying certainty has not been established.

questions.prompt: Why are scientists concerned about fish ingesting microplastics?

It can damage their digestive systems and reduce reproductive rates
It causes fish to migrate away from their habitats

questions.explanation: The professor states microplastics can damage digestive systems and reduce reproductive rates in marine animals.

questions.explanation: 'Ingest' means to take food or another substance into the body by swallowing.

questions.explanation: The professor says banning microbeads is a start but the broader problem requires international cooperation and policy changes.

passages.title: Sleep and Cognitive Performance
passages.text:
Scientists have long recognized a strong connection between sleep and cognitive performance. During sleep, the brain consolidates memories, transferring information from short-term storage to long-term memory. Without sufficient sleep, this process is disrupted, and individuals may find it harder to recall information or focus effectively.

Research suggests that sleep deprivation can also impair judgment and decision-making. Studies involving both students and professionals show that performance declines significantly after even one night of insufficient rest. Some experts compare the cognitive effects of sleep loss to those of mild alcohol intoxication.

Despite widespread awareness of these effects, many people continue to prioritize work or social activities over sleep. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable, as their biological sleep cycle naturally shifts later, yet school schedules often require early rising. Public health experts argue that adjusting school start times could improve student performance and overall well-being.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How schools can improve their teaching methods
The relationship between sleep and cognitive performance
Why professionals prefer working at night
New medical treatments for sleep disorders
questions.explanation: The passage explains how sleep affects memory, judgment, and learning ability.

questions.prompt: What happens to memory during sleep according to the passage?
options: Information is transferred from short-term to long-term memory

questions.explanation: The passage states that during sleep the brain consolidates memories by moving information from short-term to long-term storage.

options: Adolescents naturally prefer waking up early

questions.explanation: The passage explains that adolescents' biological clocks shift later, but schools still start early, suggesting a mismatch.

questions.prompt: The word 'consolidates' in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Consolidate' means to strengthen or make more solid — here referring to organizing memories for long-term retention.

passages.title: The Rise of Remote Work
passages.text:
Remote work — performing job duties from locations outside the traditional office — has expanded dramatically in recent years. While some employees worked remotely before the 2020s, widespread adoption accelerated when global events forced many businesses to close physical offices. [A]

Proponents of remote work argue that it offers greater flexibility and can improve work-life balance. Employees who work from home often report lower commuting stress and more time for personal activities. Some studies also suggest that remote workers can be more productive in focused tasks when distractions are reduced. [B]

However, critics point to significant drawbacks. Remote workers may feel isolated, and communication between colleagues can become less spontaneous and more fragmented. Managers sometimes find it challenging to monitor performance and maintain team cohesion without regular face-to-face interaction. [C] Additionally, not all job roles are suited to remote arrangements, particularly those requiring hands-on work or specialized equipment.

As businesses adapt to this evolving landscape, many have adopted hybrid models that combine in-office and remote work. [D] Whether this approach will become the new standard for professional life remains an open question, as both employers and employees continue to evaluate what works best for productivity and well-being.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: All companies now require employees to work remotely
Remote work has expanded and presents both benefits and challenges
Remote work is harmful and should be limited by law
Most employees strongly prefer working in physical offices
questions.explanation: The passage covers the growth of remote work, its advantages, drawbacks, and the emergence of hybrid models.

questions.prompt: What do some studies suggest about remote workers' productivity?
options: They are always more productive than office workers
They struggle with all types of professional tasks
They can be more productive in focused tasks when distractions are reduced
Their productivity depends entirely on internet connection quality
questions.explanation: The passage says some studies suggest remote workers can be more productive in focused tasks when distractions are reduced.

questions.prompt: What challenge do managers face with remote teams?
options: Finding reliable internet connections for staff
Maintaining team cohesion without face-to-face interaction
Managing employees across multiple office buildings
Dealing with a larger number of employees than before
questions.explanation: The passage states managers find it challenging to maintain team cohesion without regular face-to-face interaction.

questions.prompt: What does the passage imply about hybrid work models?
options: They are already proven to be the best option for all industries
They represent an ongoing compromise that is still being evaluated
They are only suitable for technology companies
They will eventually be replaced by fully remote work
questions.explanation: The passage notes hybrid models have emerged as a response, but whether they will become the standard 'remains an open question'.

questions.prompt: The word 'cohesion' in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Cohesion' refers to the quality of being united or working effectively together as a group.

questions.prompt: Where would this sentence most logically appear in the passage? 'This shift represented one of the fastest changes in workplace culture in recent history.'
questions.explanation: The sentence refers to the rapid adoption of remote work, which logically follows near [A] after the description of businesses closing offices and accelerating remote adoption.
